oil.summary: Crude marched higher for a second consecutive session, with Brent settling at $89.11/bbl (+1.58%) and WTI at $83.40/bbl (+1.55%), extending a torrid weekly run of +12.3% and +10.1% respectively. The overarching driver remains the Hormuz crisis: Iran confirmed the strait stays closed until U.S. conditions are met, while a Ukrainian drone strike on a major Russian refinery and a Houthi claim of an Aramco facility attack added fresh supply-side anxiety. Russian seaborne exports hit their lowest since May, squeezed between domestic refinery demand and physical disruption. On the demand side, Chinese teapot refiners are set to ramp Iranian barrels through Shandong as stockpiles draw down. OPEC output climbed 1.17 mb/d in July but remains below quota. RBOB was the stark outlier, cratering 7.76% on the day — an anomaly warranting close monitoring. CME options continue to price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Hormuz closure holds: Iran conditions for reopening remain unmet, keeping a geopolitical premium firmly embedded in Brent and WTI
Russian supply squeeze: seaborne exports at a May low on combined refinery-run pull and Ukrainian drone damage to domestic refinery infrastructure
Demand-side push: Chinese teapot refiners poised to accelerate Iranian crude purchases as Shandong inventories deplete

gas.summary: Henry Hub eased 0.89% on the day to $2.769/MMBtu, though the one-week gain of +3.2% suggests some residual support from the broader energy complex. TTF slipped 1.26% to €60.03/MWh after a strong monthly run of +17.1%, likely consolidating after the recent geopolitically driven surge. Headline flow for the gas sector is thin today; the single substantive story — Rystad projecting China's coal-to-gas industry to triple by 2030 as a strategic buffer against import exposure — is a long-dated structural data point rather than an immediate price catalyst. Traders should note the divergence between a softening Henry Hub and still-elevated TTF, which continues to reflect tighter European supply dynamics tied to the Hormuz shock.
drivers: TTF consolidates after a +17% monthly rally; short-term pressure from mild day-on-day profit-taking, not a fundamental reversal
Henry Hub remains subdued relative to European benchmarks, reflecting looser U.S. domestic supply conditions
Structural long-term signal: Rystad projects Chinese coal-to-gas capacity to triple by 2030, potentially reshaping LNG import demand patterns

power.summary: EU carbon edged up modestly, with EUAs gaining 0.38% to $78.21/EUA, supported by a constructive monthly trend (+2.1%) even as TTF softened intraday. The headline mover in European power today was France, where a fresh heatwave is curbing nuclear output at the continent's largest nuclear generator, triggering a reported 22% jump in French day-ahead power prices. That dynamic — reduced low-carbon baseload colliding with heat-driven demand — is supportive of both power prices and carbon. On the geopolitical overlay, Hormuz headlines continue to bleed into power markets: Iran's vow to keep the strait closed, Trump's conditional exit signals, and the IEA's assessment of a 'two-speed' global fuel price recovery all point to a persistently elevated cost-of-generation backdrop for gas-fired power across Europe. The Hormuz-related headlines in the power feed are noted but are primarily an oil and LNG supply story rather than a direct power market driver.
drivers: French nuclear curtailment: heatwave reducing output at Europe's dominant nuclear baseload supplier, driving a 22% surge in French day-ahead power prices
EUA carbon steady to firm: supportive monthly trend intact; heat-driven gas-for-power substitution and tighter supply conditions underpin the carbon price
IEA flags unsettled global fuel markets five months into the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict, keeping gas-fired generation cost uncertainty elevated across Europe
